title: IFM Investors' staff costs go past $1b as profit surges
full_text:
IFM Investors more than doubled its annual profit after significant fee growth in its infrastructure and real estate portfolios, while staff costs at the asset manager, backed by some of the country's biggest superannuation funds, surged past $1 billion last year.
IFM invests on behalf of funds such as AustralianSuper and Australian Retirement Trust. It recorded an after-tax profit of $251.5 million and grew its assets to $291 billion, making it one of the world's largest private infrastructure managers, despite a year of economic and geopolitical uncertainty.
But the asset manager has faced considerable scrutiny from its heavyweight shareholders, having held an offsite event in Sri Lanka in September because it was the "midpoint" between its various global offices, as reported by The Australian Financial Review's Rear Window column. The fund also sponsored the opening night of a separate trip to Toronto last month, billed as a study tour by the Australian Council of Superannuation Investors, creating disquiet among some of its major retirement savings fund backers.
In filings with the corporate regulator, IFM said that director pay had fallen 8 per cent to $1.6 million - following two years of increases - while chief executive David Neal's remuneration reached $3.8 million.
Employee headcount grew 2.7 per cent to 1230 people as staff expenses - including salaries, leave, bonuses and other entitlements - jumped 10 per cent to more than $1 billion. Data provided to the government last year showed the average IFM employee was paid $532,000, although that was skewed heavily by the huge performance bonuses for the investment team.
"As a global institutional asset manager, IFM Investors operates in a global marketplace, so to attract and retain the best people, it is important that we pay globally competitive remuneration," a spokesman said.
The filings, for the 12 months to June 30, are the first since IFM integrated ISPT, a superannuation fund property platform, into its business. The merger was based on the pair's overlapping ownership and "blurring of the boundaries" between asset classes such as infrastructure and property.
Cath Bowtell, the former Australian Council of Trade Unions official who now chairs IFM, said in the filings it was a year of "heightened macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty".
"Inflationary pressures, elevated interest rates, disruption to global energy markets, ongoing trade and geopolitical tensions" were present across the period, Bowtell said, adding there had been "accelerating technological change, including the continued expansion of artificial intelligence".
"Despite this environment, the group delivered strong fundraising outcomes and investment returns during 2026," Bowtell said. "The directors believe the group continues to be a resilient business and that its long-term investment approach, strong client relationships and expanding capabilities position IFM well for the future."
Revenue was bolstered primarily by higher fees from its infrastructure and real estate investments.
IFM has been actively promoting the investment capabilities of the $4.8 trillion superannuation system overseas, including in Canada, the US and Europe - pitching retirement funds as a source of capital to renew ageing infrastructure such as roads or airports.
In December, it set up an office with five employees in Toronto to deepen its roots in North America.
At the same time, the asset manager has also sought to deflect a push for retirement savings to be invested in priority areas - including renewable energy, housing and defence.
"It is not the job of industry super funds to resolve the economic issues that Australia has," IFM external relations executive David Whiteley said earlier this year. "Australian super funds can afford to be selective with their investments to get the best returns for their members."
Nine Entertainment Co.
author: Lucas Baird
